name: Vibravox
description: Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone. The dataset also includes audio data from an airborne microphone used as a reference. The Vibravox corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are also included in the corpus.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
publisher: Laboratoire de Mécanique des Structures et des Systèmes Couplés, Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, HESAM Université, Paris, France; French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis (ISL)
citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, 'vibravox (revision 071945b),' 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
rai:dataCollection: The Vibravox dataset was collected through a controlled recording protocol involving 200 participants (188 retained after post-processing). Each participant was equipped with six audio sensors simultaneously recorded using a Zoom F8n field recorder at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution. The recording process consisted of four steps per participant: (1) speech-clean: reading sentences from French Wikipedia for 15 minutes; (2) speechless-noisy: remaining silent for 2 minutes 24 seconds in a noisy environment; (3) speechless-clean: remaining silent for 54 seconds in complete silence; (4) speech-noisy: 54 seconds of speech in a noisy environment. Ambient noise was broadcast via a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers using a high-order ambisonics 3D spatializer.
rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Experiments
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained after post-processing, with 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences excluded. Issues included mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, and instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped. In some cases, such as when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, automatic filters were not triggered.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Audio recordings from six simultaneous sensors (headset microphone, forehead accelerometer, in-ear soft foam microphone, in-ear rigid earpiece microphone, throat microphone, and temple vibration pickup) recorded at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution using a Zoom F8n field recorder. Text for participant readings originated from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise samples were sourced from Audio Set and in-house recordings of concerts and street events in 3rd and 5th order ambisonics.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel to attenuate low-frequency noise and artifacts. Signals were resampled to 16 kHz for training of speech enhancement models. VAD timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; in rare cases where adjusted timestamps exceeded original audio boundaries, audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. The dataset was split by speaker with 80% in training, 10% in validation, and 10% in test sets, ensuring no speaker overlap between splits.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A series of three automatic filters were applied to the speech-clean subset: (1) PER filter: discards samples where Phoneme Error Rate > 10%, computed using Levenshtein distance between labeled and Whisper-derived phonetic transcriptions; (2) SNR filter: retains samples where SNR[i,j] = Lspeech[i,j] - Lsilence[i,j] > 1.5 dB to verify sensor functioning; (3) Sensitivity drift filter: checks that Lspeech[i,j] > Lsilence[i] to detect sensitivity drift. All audio recordings for the three other subsets (speech-noisy, speechless-clean, speechless-noisy) were systematically added if the corresponding speech-clean subset of the participant was not empty. Text was filtered to exclude proper names (except common first names, French town/region/country names), numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors. Common text normalization (lowercasing, removing punctuation except apostrophes) was applied.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Phonetic transcriptions were generated using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) with 33 French phonemes using the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. For words where the phonemizer produced language switches, manual phonetic transcription was performed. The whisper-timestamped model was used for Voice Activity Detection and word timestamp alignment during post-processing. Linguistic transcriptions from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice were retained as text labels.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Text phonemizer of the CoML lab; whisper-timestamped model (https://github.com/linto-ai/whisper-timestamped)
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Phoneme Error Rate (PER) was computed using the Levenshtein distance between labeled phonetic transcriptions and phonetic transcriptions derived from Whisper's output. Samples with PER > 10% were discarded to ensure high-quality labels. Manual phonetic transcription was performed for words unrecognized by the automatic phonemizer (e.g., 'algorithme').
rai:annotatorDemographics: 188 participants (97 female, 91 male). Mean age: 25.9 years for females, 31.4 years for males, 28.55 years overall. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped model for Voice Activity Detection and phoneme error rate computation; text phonemizer of the CoML lab for IPA phonetic transcription
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly available on HuggingFace under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. The dataset is versioned (revision 071945b referenced in citation). Code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jhauret/vibravox.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender and age of participants are collected. The dataset is GDPR-compliant with informed consent obtained, purpose of data collection clearly communicated, and anonymization and encryption of data during storage and analysis ensured.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance research in body-conducted speech capture for robust communication in noisy environments, with applications in military operations, industrial settings, voice commands, and biometric authentication. It could enable higher recognition accuracy in challenging environments and support development of communication systems for real-world applications. Potential military applications include access control and intelligence gathering.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is only in French, restricting applicability to French-language research. The Lombard effect (speakers increasing vocal effort in noisy conditions) means reported signal-to-external-noise ratios represent a lower bound on actual values. The speech-noisy subset is limited in size (approximately 1 hour 34 minutes of training data), requiring aggressive data augmentation to prevent overfitting. Some participants' ear canals were too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, affecting data quality for those sensors.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset lacks a clean reference for the speech-noisy subset, limiting its direct use for training speech enhancement models. The temple vibration pickup has a very narrow bandwidth (below 1500 Hz), limiting its utility for high-frequency speech tasks. The dataset contains only French speech, limiting generalizability to other languages. Individual variance in sensor fit (particularly for in-ear microphones) affects recording quality. The assumption that airborne and body-transmitted speech share a simple transfer function is inadequate for generating realistic synthetic data.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, Validation, and Testing for: (1) Speech enhancement / bandwidth extension using body-conduction microphones; (2) Speech-to-phonemes / automatic speech recognition; (3) Speaker verification; (4) Heart rate tracking and vital sign monitoring (using speechless-clean subset); (5) Voice commands development; (6) Comparative analysis of different body-conduction sensor technologies. The speech-noisy subset is primarily intended for testing purposes.
